seoTitle: How to Use Webflow Templates to Start a Project Fast
metaDescription: Browse, buy or clone, and customize a Webflow template, and what carries over when you do (pages and styles, not your demo CMS content or logins).
intro:
Starting a Webflow project from a template turns a blank canvas problem into an editing problem, which is a much easier place to work from. Instead of building responsive grids and a class system from nothing, you're picking a design that already works and reshaping it around your own brand and content.

Webflow splits this into two separate paths that look similar but aren't: paid Templates, bought individually, and free Cloneables shared by the community. This guide covers browsing both, what "starting from" one copies into your account, and the global styles, placeholder content, and site name you touch first once it lands in the Designer.
costNote: Templates on webflow.com/templates range from free up to roughly $150 as a one-time purchase per site. Cloneables under Made in Webflow cost nothing. Either way, you're still paying separately for whatever Webflow hosting or CMS plan the finished site needs.

steps.heading: Know which of the two you're looking at
steps.body: The template marketplace shows a grid of live preview thumbnails, each tagged with its designer, price, and a Popular or Featured badge where it applies. Prices run from free up through premium layouts in the $79-plus range. But not every free-looking entry works the same way: templates from webflow.com/templates are bought and licensed per site, while Cloneables under Made in Webflow are shared by the community at no cost and use a different button entirely, Clone in Webflow, instead of a purchase flow. Check which section you're in before you commit to one.

image.caption: The Webflow template marketplace grid, showing preview thumbnails, designer credits, and prices ranging from free to premium.

steps.heading: Open the in-Designer Templates picker
steps.body: If you're starting a new site instead of browsing standalone, the Templates modal inside the dashboard offers the same catalog organized differently: a sidebar splits it into All templates, Recommended, and Style guides, followed by industry categories like Technology, Portfolio & Agency, Blog & Editorial, and Professional Services. This is the faster route once you already know roughly what kind of site you're building, since you can jump straight to a category instead of scrolling the full marketplace.

image.caption: The Templates modal's category sidebar and grid, grouping options like Business Starter and Nextconf under sections such as Blog & Editorial.

steps.heading: Buy or clone it, then name your site
steps.body:
For a paid template, the flow runs through your Dashboard: New site, Choose Template, then the Purchased filter to find one you already own. For a free Cloneable, it's View details, then Clone in Webflow, then a Workspace to add it to. Either way, the next thing Webflow asks for is a site name, prefilled with something generic worth replacing right away since it becomes part of your default subdomain.

What lands in your account is pages, styles, components, interactions, and uploaded assets. It is not the demo CMS entries (blog posts, portfolio items, product listings), form submissions, API keys, or any third-party integration credentials the original had wired up. Those you build or reconnect yourself.

image.caption: The "Name your site" dialog that appears after starting from a template, prefilled with a placeholder name to replace.

steps.heading: Open the new project and get oriented
steps.body: Once it's ready, Webflow drops you into the Designer with the template fully built out: navigation, hero section, and page structure all in place and editable. Take a pass through the Navigator panel on the left first to see how the original designer organized sections and classes before changing anything, since that structure varies a lot between templates. Click into the main heading or hero text to confirm you can select and edit it cleanly, a quick sanity check that everything came through intact.

image.caption: A cloned ecommerce template open in the Designer, with the hero heading selected and the page's section structure visible in the Navigator.

steps.heading: Update global styles to match your brand
steps.body: Open the project's style guide or global classes and change the core brand elements: heading fonts, body text, button colors, and any color variables the template defined, before touching individual sections. Templates are built around a small set of reusable classes specifically so a handful of global edits ripple across the whole site instead of requiring section-by-section restyling. Doing this first also means you're previewing your own colors and fonts as you write, not the designer's placeholder palette.

steps.heading: Replace placeholder content and rebuild any CMS collections
steps.body: Work through each page swapping stock photography and lorem ipsum for your own copy and imagery, watching image aspect ratios since templates often crop tightly and a mismatched replacement distorts the layout. If the template includes CMS collections, remember step three: the demo entries didn't come with it, so check how the fields are structured before adding your own, since renaming or removing a field the layout depends on can break the display.

steps.heading: Check responsive breakpoints and publish
steps.body: Switch through the tablet, mobile landscape, and mobile portrait views before publishing, since content swaps and font changes can shift spacing in ways that only show up at smaller widths. Fix anything that overlaps or overflows, update each page's SEO title and meta description, then publish. A template gets you most of the way to a finished site fast, but the responsive pass is what keeps it looking intentional instead of obviously templated.

tables.title: Templates vs. Cloneables
rows: Free to roughly $150, one-time per site
Dashboard → New site → Choose Template → Purchased
tables.note: Both leave CMS content, form submissions, and third-party integration credentials behind; only structure and design copy over.

troubleshooting.problem: The cloned or purchased site is missing the blog posts, products, or portfolio items shown in the preview
troubleshooting.cause: Starting a site from a template copies pages, styles, components, and uploaded assets, but not CMS collection items, form submissions, or integration credentials.
troubleshooting.fix: Populate the CMS collections yourself, matching the field structure the template already defines, instead of deleting and rebuilding it.

troubleshooting.problem: There's no Clone in Webflow button on a template worth using
troubleshooting.cause: It's a paid Template, not a free Cloneable. Paid templates are purchased and started from your Dashboard, not cloned directly from a preview page.
troubleshooting.fix: Check whether the design lives under Made in Webflow (free, clonable) or Templates (paid, purchased through the Dashboard's New site flow).

troubleshooting.problem: Duplicating a finished site built from a premium template asks you to pay again
troubleshooting.cause: Webflow's own help documentation states that duplicating a site using a purchased template requires repurchasing that template's license for the duplicate.
troubleshooting.fix: Budget for a second license if a true duplicate is needed, or start the second site from the same source template instead of copying the finished one.

faq.question: Do I need to pay for every Webflow template?
faq.answer: No. The marketplace mixes free Cloneables with paid Templates that typically offer more advanced layouts, richer CMS structures, or ecommerce setups already built in.

faq.question: What's the actual difference between a Template and a Cloneable?
faq.answer: Templates are sold through webflow.com/templates by vetted designers and started from your Dashboard after purchase. Cloneables are free, community-made projects under Made in Webflow, started with a Clone in Webflow button instead.

faq.question: Does starting from a template bring over its demo content and images?
faq.answer: The structure does: pages, styles, components, interactions, and uploaded assets. The demo CMS entries, form submissions, API keys, and third-party integration credentials do not carry over.

faq.question: Can I change a template's layout structure completely?
faq.answer: Yes. Once it's in your account, it's a normal Webflow project, so you can rearrange sections, delete elements, or restructure pages just like a site built from scratch.

faq.question: Will editing a template break its responsive design?
faq.answer: It can, especially after swapping images or lengthening text, so check each breakpoint after major changes to confirm spacing and alignment still hold up.

faq.question: If I duplicate a site built from a paid template, do I pay for the template again?
faq.answer: Yes, according to Webflow's help documentation. A duplicate of a site using a purchased template needs its own license.
